title: The real transport matching theorem
subtitle: Independent reading companion to G3 025000
adaptation: Edited G3 lecture prose restructured into readable slide units; formulas and selected SVG geometric models are authored companion material.

slides.title: The central problem
slides.lead: The canonical direct rotation need not minimize an unsquared Schatten norm of whole-space displacement among all real orthogonal maps transporting one subspace onto another.
body: A four-dimensional example with two equal principal angles refutes the broad claim. A useful positive problem remains: characterize the global minimum when the exponent p is strictly between one and two.

slides.title: What are we optimizing?
slides.lead: Take two subspaces K and L of equal finite dimension inside a real Euclidean space.
body: Consider every orthogonal operator U that maps K onto L. Measure its displacement from the identity using a Schatten p norm. Concretely, take every singular value of the difference between U and the identity, raise it to power p, add, and then take the pth root. For p equal two, this is the Frobenius norm. For p equal one, it is the nuclear or trace norm. When p lies strictly between one and two, the contribution of a set of singular values differs from its squared-energy contribution.

slides.title: What are we optimizing? · further detail
slides.lead: That is precisely where the direct rotation can lose optimality.
body: Why do we require equal dimensions? An invertible orthogonal map preserves dimension. If K and L have different dimensions, no such U maps one onto the other, regardless of how close their projections might be. We would first need a different admissible notion of transport.

slides.title: The single principal-angle block
slides.lead: Begin with a single principal angle theta between two lines.
body: In their common real two-dimensional principal plane, an orthogonal rotation through theta maps the first line to the second. Its displacement operator has two equal singular values, each equal to twice sine of theta over two. Therefore its pth power Schatten cost is two times the quantity twice sine theta over two, raised to power p. There is a choice of the sign of the rotation, but its singular values are the same. Reflections can also map one line to the other.

slides.title: The single principal-angle block · further detail
slides.lead: Their displacement costs may differ, so the full optimization must allow all orthogonal transports, not just orientation-preserving rotations.
body: With two or more principal angles, a naive strategy would minimize the cost in each principal plane independently and sum.

slides.title: The single principal-angle block · continued
slides.lead: That works for some objectives, but our four-dimensional counterexample demonstrated a failure of unrestricted independent-plane optimality.
body: The missing degree of freedom is a coupling between two principal-angle blocks. A four-dimensional orthogonal operator can mix their coordinates while still mapping the entire source subspace onto the target. It might produce a more favorable distribution of displacement singular values under the chosen exponent.

slides.title: Why a matching appears
slides.lead: The real transport optimization turns that freedom into a finite combinatorial problem.
body: Label the positive principal angles. Each label can remain a singleton, carrying the best permitted one-angle cost, or it can be paired with another label, carrying the best two-angle cost from a four-dimensional block. A matching consists of disjoint pairs together with unmatched singletons. Represent it by a permutation that equals its own inverse: a fixed point denotes a singleton, and a two-cycle a paired block. No angle label can belong to two different pairs. The cost of a matching is the sum of singleton weights and complete pair weights. If we sum over all labels rather than over edges, each pair contributes half its full weight at each endpoint, so it is counted exactly once.
slides.formula: each label remains a singleton or forms a disjoint pair

slides.title: Why a matching appears · continued
slides.lead: The minimum over all matchings exists because the set of involutive permutations of finitely many labels is finite.
body: This is a substantial simplification. Instead of optimizing over a continuum of orthogonal matrices all at once, we can evaluate finitely many candidate matchings, where the difficult continuous optimization has been absorbed into the one-angle and two-angle weights.

slides.title: An exact two-angle test
slides.lead: Suppose the positive principal angles are theta and psi.
body: There are two combinatorial candidates. One leaves both labels unmatched. Its cost is the sum of the two singleton costs. The other pairs them, and its cost is a single optimized four-dimensional value. The global minimum is the smaller of those two numbers. For p equal two, the squared Frobenius objective is tied directly to the sum of squared displacements, and the canonical direct rotation satisfies the established squared-objective theorem. For exponents strictly between one and two, the paired option can be better. The optimized cost of a paired block need not equal the cost of the direct rotation acting independently on its two principal planes. The correct pair cost minimizes over both relevant four-dimensional determinant classes.

slides.title: An exact two-angle test · continued
slides.lead: Replacing it with the direct rotation's candidate cost would assert an optimality property that fails for the unsquared objective.
body: For three positive angles, the finite choices are: three singletons, or one pair and one singleton. For four, we also have two disjoint pairs. In general, the number of matchings grows, but the mathematical structure stays finite and explicit.

slides.title: The two directions of an optimality proof
slides.lead: A formula for the minimum needs two distinct inequalities.
body: First, every admissible real orthogonal transporter must have a displacement cost at least the matching minimum. Second, every candidate matching, or at least an optimal matching, must be realizable by a genuine orthogonal transporter with exactly the assigned cost. The first direction is an extraction theorem. It analyzes an ambient optimizer and shows that its cost is represented by suitable singleton and paired blocks, preserving the original principal-angle labels. The second direction is a realization theorem. It assembles orthogonal blocks into an ambient transporter with the required action on the source subspace. Neither direction can be replaced merely by noting that the minimum of finitely many numbers exists. A combinatorial optimizer might describe no actual geometric operator unless realization is proved.

slides.title: The two directions of an optimality proof · continued
slides.lead: Conversely, a construction of candidate transports does not rule out a more exotic, lower-cost orthogonal matrix.
body: The result combines two arguments in finite-dimensional real spaces with equal-dimensional subspaces and Schatten exponent p strictly between one and two: a lower bound extracting matching data from every ambient optimizer, and an upper bound constructing an orthogonal transporter from an optimizing matching. Repeated and zero principal angles remain legitimate labeled inputs.

slides.title: Why the exponent matters
slides.lead: The nuclear norm is the sum of singular values, and the Frobenius norm comes from their squared sum.
body: A cost that is additive in squared singular values rewards a different distribution than a cost that is additive in singular values themselves. Between powers one and two, changing the singular-value distribution by mixing principal planes can be advantageous. This is why one must name the exponent in an optimality theorem. The best operator for one Schatten norm need not minimize another.

slides.title: Why the exponent matters · further detail
slides.lead: The direct rotation's optimality for a squared objective does not imply its optimality for an unsquared objective, even though the underlying pair of subspaces is identical.
body: There are also delicate endpoint questions. A theorem proved for exponents strictly between one and two should not be quoted as automatically covering p equal one or p equal two. Continuity of an optimized value can help study endpoint costs, but a complete endpoint statement may need its own realization and attainment arguments.

slides.title: Scope of the matching theorem
slides.lead: For real finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with equal-dimensional source and target subspaces, and Schatten exponent p strictly between one and two, there is an orthogonal transporter attaining the matching minimum.
body: Every admissible orthogonal transporter has pth-power displacement cost at least this value, and an optimizing matching can be realized geometrically. The assumptions include finite dimension, a real inner product, equal source and target dimension, and p strictly between one and two. The conclusion concerns the pth power of the Schatten norm of identity minus the transporter; taking the pth root preserves comparisons because p is positive. The theorem does not state a universal result for arbitrary symmetric gauges or every exponent. To reconstruct the argument, begin with principal planes, calculate the two equal singular values of a planar rotation, state the optimized one- and two-angle costs, and prove that any matching can be assembled by orthogonal direct sum.

slides.title: Scope of the matching theorem · continued
slides.lead: Then identify the genuinely difficult converse: ruling out an ambient transport more efficient than every matching.
body: That converse is why this is a mathematical theorem rather than a convenient search heuristic. The matching theorem supplies a positive classification for the stated real Schatten optimization problem. Its assumptions on dimension, rank, and exponent remain part of the claim.
slides.takeaway: The real p-Schatten problem for 1 < p < 2 reduces to realizable singleton and pair matchings.
